newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to fight corruption without emergency steps.
newsitem.headline: Russia to fight corruption without emergency steps.

text.p: Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, tackling a deep-rooted problem that has been the scourge of Russia for centuries, vowed on Tuesday to crack down on corruption and halt the growth of a huge shadow economy.

The conservative minister, discarding the general's uniform he usually wears for a dark civilian suit, set out plans to prevent tax evasion under new powers bestowed on him by President Boris Yeltsin to smash economic crime.
He said crimes such as corruption, which persisted despite efforts to root it out in tsarist and communist days, were rife but vowed not to revert to emergency measures to crack down.

"The president's decision (to promote me) was dictated by the complexity of the economic situation...and the increasing criminalisation of the economy," Kulikov told a news conference marking his promotion to deputy prime minister on February 4.
"All these facts create social tensions and unfortunately prompt a growth in the number of strikes and hunger strikes and other protest actions."
But Kulikov, whose new duties give him control of the tax police and all agencies fighting economic crime, declared: "I am categorically opposed to extraordinary measures."

Russian officials acknowledge that a surge in crime since the collapse in the Soviet Union in 1991, some of it carried out by criminal gangs and much of it involving the economy, is a problem which discourages foreign investors.
Kulikov's promotion prompted speculation that the government woudl finally match pledges to get tough on economic crime with decisive action.
He said after talks with Yeltsin last week that he had been given "carte blanche" in his new role.

Interfax news agency has also said that Yeltsin, who came to power in 1991 vowing to wipe out abuse of power, will announce urgent measures to weed out corruption in his annual address to parliament on March 6.
But the 50-year-old minister's comments on Tuesday indicated he would concentrate, at least for now, on simply coordinating the various forces which are already fighting economic crime.
Kulikov said only 16 percent of Russian companies met their full tax obligations last year.
"This shows we need a united approach and strategy, and that one organ must be in control and coordinate," he said.
Cooperation should be improved with Russia's border guards, the foreign intelligence service, the counter-intelligence network and the Procurator General's office, he said.

Kulikov said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had approved his initiative to make an inventory of tax privileges, which cost the state billions of dollars a year, and that the cabinet would discuss a draft new tax code on Thursday.
But he painted a bleak picture and said a vast illegal and unregulated shadow economy was growing.
"If the situation does not change in the next two to three years, the shadow economy will account for 40 percent of the country's economy," he said, echoing Chernomyrdin's predictions.
The government has made improvement of tax collection a priority and launched a television campaign to back its efforts.
Official figures show that tax arrears rose to 128.25 trillion roubles ($23 billion) at the start of this year, more than twice the level at the start of 1996.
The bad tax revenues prompted the International Monetary Fund to withhold two tranches of credit late last year, and it relented only when more tax money started to come in.
The government says tax evasion is a prime cause of delays in the payment of wages and pensions which have prompted widespread disillusionment and anger across Russia.
